The PAINT Act aligns with S.1717—the Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act—which mandates Medicare coverage for breakthrough devices during a 4-year transitional period. While streamlining access is critical, the $10M annual funding allocation for CMS program management (Sec.2(c)) raises questions about bureaucratic overhead versus direct patient benefit.

True efficiency requires sunsetting redundant approval layers entirely, not just creating new compliance checkpoints. Medicare’s track record of delayed national coverage determinations (Sec.1862(l)(2)) proves more structural reform is needed beyond procedural tweaks.

Cutting red tape shouldn’t mean shuffling it through different agency desks. Let’s audit implementation costs in real-time to ensure savings actually reach patients instead of feeding administrative bloat.

The real test is whether these reforms deliver care or just more paperwork—see the full analysis: https://t.co/plA9UGO6sM

The PAINT Act sounds good on paper—streamlining Medicare access to breakthrough medical tech. But let’s not kid ourselves: unless it slashes the red tape Big Pharma and D.C. bureaucrats love, it’s just another bill that sounds pro-patient while letting insiders game the system.

Medicare already burns $800B annually, with billions lost to fraud and overpriced contracts. If this doesn’t include strict audits on device pricing and a ban on revolving-door lobbyists writing the rules, it’s performative.

Innovation shouldn’t mean blank checks to corporations while taxpayers foot the bill. Cut the waste first, then talk access.

The real test is whether this bill puts patients first or just fattens industry margins—see the receipts: https://t.co/eCPnO7fN7D
